title: Dramatic Scenes, and Other Poems
description: The first published volume of the barrister-poet who wrote under the name Barry Cornwall, issued anonymously in 1819 and made up of short dramatic monologues and lyric pieces spoken by imagined persons in moments of strong feeling. The Dramatic Scenes give voice to lovers, mothers, outcasts, and historical or legendary figures in a single sustained utterance, while the Other Poems add songs and meditations on nature, memory, and death. The volume established the quiet, sympathetic, and deliberately unobtrusive manner that made Cornwall one of the most reprinted poets of the 1820s and 1830s.
plot_or_argument: The volume has no continuous plot; it presents a gallery of soliloquies and lyrics. In the dramatic pieces a speaker addresses an absent or present listener at the crisis of a passion: a lover pleading or mourning, a parent sorrowing for a child, a rejected or exile figure declaring inner pain. The lyrics turn on recollection, the consolation of natural scenery, the pity aroused by human suffering, and the peace found in resignation. Recurring situations are patient endurance of wrong, the sanctity of tender feeling, and sympathy with the lowly and the erring.
narrative_structure: A collection ordered loosely by kind, the dramatic soliloquies occupying the opening and the shorter lyrics and sonnets following; each poem is a self-contained utterance with no framing narrative linking the numbers, so the progression is thematic rather than sequential.
principal_characters: lover-speakers lamenting parted or lost affection; a mourning parent; an outcast or exile pleading his cause; the meditative lyric speaker contemplating nature, memory, and death
literary_form: Dramatic lyric and soliloquy gathered in a miscellaneous volume; poems of feeling in the manner of the period's humanitarian verse
meter_and_prosody: Chiefly regular lyric stanzas and blank-verse meditations in iambic pentameter, with some sonnets; the diction is simple, musical, and deliberately free of obscurity, and the prosody is smooth and end-stopped rather than experimental.
historical_context: Published in the post-Waterloo decade when a humane, sympathetic verse of feeling circulated alongside the more radical and the more sublime modes of Romanticism. The author, a bench lawyer, wrote in the circle of Charles Lamb and of the Ollier publishing house that also issued the works of Keats and of Leigh Hunt; the volume appeared anonymously in an age when a poet of feeling could win readers without a famous name.
literary_significance: The volume announced Barry Cornwall as a leading voice of the gentle, sympathetic current in Romantic verse, and its dramatic soliloquies look forward to the Victorian dramatic monologue. Its reprints and its praise by contemporaries, including the pre-Raphaelites, kept humanitarian lyric of feeling before the reading public through the century.
attribution_notes: Published anonymously in 1819; the authorship by Bryan Waller Procter under the literary name Barry Cornwall is established by later collected editions and by the author's own acknowledgement.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1819, C. and J. Ollier, in octavo; a second edition followed in 1820, and the pieces were later gathered into the collected Poems of Barry Cornwall.

title: English Songs, and Other Small Poems
description: A volume of short lyric songs and small poems by Barry Cornwall, issued in 1832 and gathering the compact, singable pieces for which the poet was best remembered by later Victorian readers. The songs treat love, parting, home, childhood, and the consolation of nature in an artless, melodious style that courts the air of the traditional English song. It is the clearest statement of Cornwall's gift for the brief lyric and the volume from which several of his songs passed into nineteenth-century anthologies and into recitation.
plot_or_argument: The book has no argument; it is a sequence of independent lyrics. Individual songs address a beloved, lament absent or lost love, welcome sleep or the evening, recall the pleasures of childhood and home, or draw a gentle moral from a natural scene such as the falling of leaves or the sound of bells. The tone throughout is tender, melancholy, and resigned, with feeling kept within the limits of the simple song rather than carried to meditation or narrative.
narrative_structure: A miscellaneous collection of separate short songs and poems with no ordering principle or framing narrative; the reader moves from one self-contained lyric to the next, with variety supplied by changes of speaker, occasion, and mood rather than by sequence.
principal_characters: the lover who sings of presence and absence; the mourner of lost love or youth; the child or the voice recalling home; the speaker who draws comfort from evening, sleep, and natural scenes
literary_form: Lyric song-book: short stanzic poems written to be sung or recited, in the popular English-song tradition revived by Romantic poets
meter_and_prosody: Chiefly regular song stanzas in common and short measure with simple recurring rhyme schemes, framed for melody and repetition; the lines are short, the accents even, and the diction deliberately plain and musical so as to imitate and renew the old English song.
historical_context: Published at the close of the Romantic period, when the anthology and the recited song were reaching a wide middle-class readership and when Romantic lyricists were returning to the brief, singable lyric as a counterpoise to the long meditative poem. Cornwall's songs belong to this current of humane, melodic verse, and the volume appeared as his reputation as a poet of feeling was being consolidated by the collected editions.
literary_significance: The volume preserved the short Romantic song as a living form and supplied later anthologies and reciters with some of Cornwall's most quoted lyrics; its emphasis on melody, simplicity, and sympathetic feeling anticipates the Victorian lyric song and shaped his reception as a poet of the heart rather than of the intellect.
attribution_notes: Published under the author's name as Barry Cornwall; the volume's authorship by Bryan Waller Procter is established and undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1832, Edward Moxon, in duodecimo; the pieces were later absorbed into the collected Poems of Barry Cornwall and reprinted in nineteenth-century song and poetry anthologies.

title: The World before the Flood: A Poem, in Ten Cantos
description: A long narrative and descriptive poem on the antediluvian world before the Deluge, by the Sheffield poet and editor James Montgomery, first published in 1813. The poem peopled the generations from Cain to Noah with the inventions of a Romantic imagination reading Genesis as a lost golden age of giants, agriculture, music, and crime. Its grand sweeps of the primeval earth and its moral of corrupt innocence made it one of the most widely read Biblical poems of its day and the work that established Montgomery's reputation.
plot_or_argument: The poem moves through the ten antediluvian generations. It pictures the descendants of Cain building cities, inventing music, metalwork, and agriculture, and rising into a mighty and beautiful but doomed civilisation, while the sons of Seth remain apart in innocence. A race of giants and kings grows in wealth and in violence; the daughters of men mingle with the fallen ones; and the earth fills with corruption and blood. The poem closes with Noah's warning long rejected, the coming of the flood, and the destruction of the world that had seemed so glorious, leaving the moral that splendour without righteousness perishes.
narrative_structure: A continuous narrative in ten cantos, arranged generationally and thematically rather than around a single hero; each canto opens a new phase of the primeval history, and the whole builds from creation of a culture to its catastrophic end, framed by prophecy and warning.
principal_characters: the Cainite line of Tubal-cain, Jabal, and the giant kings; Noah the preaching monitor; the sons of Seth and the daughters of men; the fallen watchers; the ruined antediluvian people
literary_form: Biblical and Miltonic narrative poem in rhymed stanzas, treating a scriptural subject as Romantic descriptive epic
meter_and_prosody: Written in a sustained stanzaic measure derived from the Spenserian and Thomsonian tradition, in smooth iambic lines with an elaborate rhyme scheme, suited to swelling description and moral reflection rather than to dramatic speech.
historical_context: Published in 1813, the poem belongs to the enduring vogue for long Biblical and 'secondary epic' poems and to the taste for the sublime and the primitive that carried over from the late eighteenth century. Montgomery, a Unitarian preacher turned Sheffield editor, had made his name with radical journalism and hymn-writing, and the poem marks his movement into the Romantic descriptive mode on a scriptural subject.
literary_significance: The poem established Montgomery as a poet of popular Religious Narrative Poetry and gave the antediluvian subject its most circulating Romantic treatment; contemporaries ranked its descriptive passages alongside Thomson and it remained a staple of the gift-book and school anthology through the century. It is a key example of how Biblical history was reimagined as a lost age of sublimity and guilt.
attribution_notes: Published with the author's name; Montgomery's authorship is undisputed. The poem is a single-author work issued in ten cantos.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1813, for Longman, Hurst, Rees, Orme, and Brown, in octavo, in ten cantos, and frequently reprinted and gathered into Montgomery's collected poetical works.

title: Greenland, and Other Poems
description: A volume of poems by James Montgomery of Sheffield, published in 1819, whose title piece is a melancholy meditation on the vanished Norwegian colony of Greenland. The volume mixes the descriptive and missionary imagination with lyric and moral pieces, reflecting Montgomery's double life as a radical editor and a hymn-writer. Greenland itself, the chief poem, imagines the lost settlements of the Norse in the frozen north and the extinguished Christian community that once flourished there, turning topography into an elegy for a perished people.
plot_or_argument: The title poem traces the rise and disappearance of the old Norse settlements in Greenland: the faith and labour of the colonists, their isolation and gradual extinction, and the modern traveller who finds only ruins, ice, and the Inhabitant where a Christian people had been. The companion poems of the volume move among moral, descriptive, and sentimental subjects, several touched by Montgomery's interest in missions, distant lands, and the transience of human establishments.
narrative_structure: A miscellaneous volume dominated by the single long descriptive-elegiac poem Greenland, with shorter lyric and moral pieces grouped after it; there is no continuous plot across the volume, and Greenland itself proceeds as a historical meditation from settlement to ruin rather than as a story with characters in action.
principal_characters: the lost Norse colonists of Greenland; the extinguished Christian settlement; the modern traveller or speaker who surveys the ruins; the Inuit inhabitant met in the emptied land
literary_form: Descriptive and elegiac poem in the Thomsonian and mission-inspired mode, gathered with shorter lyrics in a miscellaneous volume
meter_and_prosody: Greenland is written in smooth iambic pentameter couplets suited to swelling description and moral reflection; the accompanying lyrics use regular song and hymn stanzas with simple rhyme, the whole marked by Montgomery's clear, tuneful, and unforced prosody.
historical_context: Published in 1819, when the Arctic, the vanished Norse settlements, and the great missionary societies were vivid topics for a reading public fascinated by lost civilisations and distant heathendom. Montgomery, editor of the Sheffield Register and a committed Evangelical, wrote within a current that joined Romantic topographical melancholy to a missionary and humanitarian interest in perished and un evangelised peoples.
literary_significance: The volume is the principal example of Montgomery's Romantic descriptive verse and of his poetry of vanished peoples and missionary sympathy; Greenland gave the lost Norse colony its best-known English poetic treatment of the period and helped fix the vanished-settlement theme in Romantic literature of the North.
attribution_notes: Published with the author's name; Montgomery's authorship of the volume and of Greenland is undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1819, for Longman, Hurst, Rees, Orme, and Brown (printed by Strahan and Spottiswoode), in octavo; the poems were later reprinted in Montgomery's collected poetical works.

title: The Descent of Liberty: A Mask
alternative_titles: The Descent of Liberty: A Mask; with Poems
description: A political allegorical mask by Leigh Hunt, written to celebrate the peace that followed the fall of Napoleon and first published in 1815 in a volume that also gathered shorter verses. The personified Liberty descends from heaven to a Europe exhausted by war, and the poem passes in vision over the ruined and the recovering lands before turning to hopes for England and to Hunt's own imprisonment for libel. It is a characteristic piece of Hunt's radical-liberal Romanticism, joining the masque allegory of Spenser and Milton to contemporary protest against the Holy Alliance and for national freedom.
plot_or_argument: In an introductoryInvocation the spirit of Liberty is summoned; she descends and surveys a Europe scorched by the long Revolutionary and Napoleonic wars, mourning the liberties that have been betrayed by tyrants and restored monarchs. The mask passes in allegorical pageant through the fates of nations, contrasts the promise of freedom with its post-war disappointment, and ends in a brighter vision of liberty's future return and a personal note in which the imprisoned poet claims his suffering for the cause of free speech.
narrative_structure: A dramatic-allegorical mask in rhymed stanzas, framed by an invocation and unfolding as a procession of visions and personified abstractions rather than a plot of individual characters; the movement is from descent and survey through lament to prophetic hope.
principal_characters: the personified Liberty; War and its victims; the tyrants and restored kings of the post-war settlement; the poet-spectator who is also the imprisoned Leigh Hunt
literary_form: Political allegorical mask in the Romantic reviving of the Spenserian and Miltonic masque, published with accompanying shorter poems
meter_and_prosody: Chiefly Spenserian stanzas and other elaborate rhymed measures in smooth iambic lines, the ornamented stanza forms of the allegorical mask chosen for their musical and decorative effect; Hunt's easy, tuned versification is prominent rather than weighty.
historical_context: Written in 1814-15 to greet the peace and published the year of Waterloo and the Congress of Vienna, the mask expresses Hunt's Liberal hope that liberty would triumph over despotism and his fear that the settlement would only enthrone new tyrants. Hunt wrote it in the aftermath of his two-year imprisonment in Dorchester Gaol for libelling the Prince Regent, an experience that made him a byword for the Romantic literary radicalism associated with the Examiner.
literary_significance: The mask is a central document of Hunt's political Romanticism and of the liberal-allegorical current that ran alongside the more Tory or apolitical strand of the period's verse; it shows how the older masque was retooled for contemporary protest, and it shaped the younger Hazlitt, Keats, and Shelley's sense of a poetry of liberty and sensuous fancy.
attribution_notes: Published with the author's name; Leigh Hunt's authorship is undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1815, printed for Gale, Curtis, and Fenner, Paternoster Row, in octavo, forming the principal poem of a volume that included shorter verses; a Philadelphia edition appeared in 1816.

title: Foliage; or, Poems Original and Translated
description: A collection of short poems, translations, and familiar verses by Leigh Hunt, published in 1818 and giving its name to the volume that gathered much of his best-known lyric work. Foliage mixes original songs, sonnets, and meditations with translations from the Italian and with verse rendered from other languages, and it opens with the poem 'Foliage' itself, a protest against the pride of authorship and a plea for the humble, unassertive gift of poetry. The volume is the chief treasury of Hunt's lyric manner: graceful, sympathetic, and tuned to the pleasure and pity of ordinary feeling.
plot_or_argument: The volume presents no continuous argument but a range of pieces: the opening 'Foliage' reflects on the poet's dependence and the modest offering of verse; songs and sonnets treat love, friendship, absence, and death; meditations draw feeling from natural scenes and from the sight of suffering; and the translations render Italian and other poetry into English. Together they assemble Hunt's creed of a poetry of simple, humane, sensuous truth.
narrative_structure: A miscellaneous collection ordered loosely by kind and length, the programmatic 'Foliage' standing first, followed by lyric, sonnet, meditation, and translation; the reader moves piece to piece with no framing narrative.
principal_characters: the meditative lyric speaker; friends and the absent beloved; the figures of the translated and Italian pieces
literary_form: Miscellaneous lyric volume of original songs, sonnets, and meditations with translations, chiefly from the Italian
meter_and_prosody: Original and translated pieces in varied lyric stanzas, sonnets, and smooth iambic measures; Hunt's prosody is easy, musical, and end-stopped, favouring sweetness and regularity over experiment, and the translations strive to keep the lilt of their originals.
historical_context: Published in 1818 by Taylor and Hessey, the volume appeared at the height of Hunt's influence over the younger Romantics and of the Hunt circle's activity in publishing and criticism; it collects work from the years of the Examiner and of Hunt's imprisonment and reflects the Italian vogue the circle was promoting.
literary_significance: Foliage is the principal collection of Hunt's lyric verse and the source of many of his most reprinted poems; its opening address on the unpretentious gift of poetry became a statement of Hunt's poetics and of the sympathetic, familiar current of Romantic lyric associated with his name and with Keats's early allegiance to him.
attribution_notes: Published with the author's name; Hunt's authorship of the original poems and his editorship of the translations are undisputed. The volume is Hunt's, not, as has sometimes been confused, Shelley's.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1818, for Taylor and Hessey, Fleet Street, in octavo, gathering original poems and translations; reprinted within Hunt's collected Poetical Works.

title: The Fancy: A Selection from the Poetical Remains of the Late Peter Corcoran, Esq., of Gray's Inn, Student at Law
description: A volume of verse by John Hamilton Reynolds, published in 1820 under the playful fiction that it was selected from the poetical remains of an imaginary Gray's Inn lawyer named Peter Corcoran. The Fancy gathers lighter, fantastical, and Keatsian pieces, including the title poem and Reynolds's characteristic medley of song, ballad, and descriptive fancy, and it appeared in the same year and from the same publisher as Keats's own first volume. The book is the principal record of Reynolds's charm as a poet of romantic fantasy and playful sensibility, and it belonged to the circle of Hunt and the younger Romantics.
plot_or_argument: The volume has no continuous plot; it presents a series of short imaginative pieces governed by fancy rather than argument. Its poems conjure castles, old romances, moonlight, music, and melancholy scenes, treating love, loss, and the lure of the imaginary with a wistful playfulness; the frame of the fictional 'Peter Corcoran' lets Reynolds offer verse of fantasy and feeling under a humorous mask.
narrative_structure: A miscellaneous collection of short lyrics, songs, and fanciful meditations presented as the remains of an invented predecessor; the ordering is thematic and playful rather than narrative, and the framing conceit supplies unity in place of plot.
principal_characters: the fanciful lyric speaker; the invented Peter Corcoran as framing persona; the lovers, mourners, and romantic figures of the separate pieces
literary_form: Volume of romantic fantasy verse, songs, and lyric meditations under a playful fictional frame
meter_and_prosody: Chiefly light lyric stanzas, songs, and ballad measures in smooth musical iambics, with some sonnets; the versification is graceful, tuneful, and deliberately fanciful, close in manner to Keats's early verse and to Hunt's sweetness.
historical_context: Published London, 1820, by Taylor and Hessey in the same circle and season as Keats's Poems and Reynolds's friendship with Keats and the Hunt group; the fictional 'Peter Corcoran' device reflects the playful, clubbable literary culture of the period's young Romantic poets around Hunt, Reynolds, and Keats.
literary_significance: The Fancy is Reynolds's chief claim on the attention of literary history and the volume by which he is remembered chiefly as Keats's friend and fellow-author of 1820; its play of romantic fantasy exemplifies the lighter, sensuous current of the Hunt circle's verse and helps chart the milieu out of which Keats's own first book emerged.
attribution_notes: Published under Reynolds's name behind the fictional pretence of the remains of 'Peter Corcoran'; Reynolds's authorship is established and undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1820, for Taylor and Hessey, Fleet Street, in octavo, in the 'Peter Corcoran' frame; Reynolds's verse was later gathered by editors of Keats's circle and of Hunt's Anthology.

title: The Feast of the Poets; with Notes, and Other Pieces in Verse
description: A mock-heroic verse satire by Leigh Hunt, first published in the Reflector in 1811 and issued as a separate poem with notes and other pieces in verse in 1814. The poem imagines a banquet to which the living British and classical poets are summoned, and, in the manner of the Dunciad and of Scottish Burns's 'Epistle to the Old Poets', treats the guest-list of contemporary verse as a comic feast of presences and conspicuous absences. Its courteous wit, its critical as well as playful manner, and its copious annotation made it a widely-quoted document of Regency literary taste.
plot_or_argument: An invitation goes out to a feast of the poets at which the muses and their votaries gather; the poem names, praises, gently derides, or pointedly omits the poets of the day from Wordsworth and Coleridge to Rogers, Moore, and Byron. Classical poets are also invited, and the moderns are contrasted with the ancients in a running comic comparison. The notes expand the poem into a critical gloss on contemporary reputations, and the accompanying pieces in verse extend Hunt's manner into lighter lyrics.
narrative_structure: A single mock-heroic poem in rhymed couplets preceded by a brief epistle-like opening and followed by a set of explanatory notes and shorter verses; the design is episodic, moving through the guest-list of poets, and the prose notes carry much of the critical content.
principal_characters: the poet-host who presides at the feast; the invited contemporary poets of Regency England; the classical poets who appear for comparison
literary_form: Mock-heroic and critical verse satire in the Augustan tradition, revived in Regency England with a lighter, more sociable manner
meter_and_prosody: Written chiefly in smooth heroic couplets, following the Pope-Byron line of Augustan satire in a lighter, conversational tempo; the diction is witty and allusive, and the poem's argumentative edge is carried in the couplet as often as in the notes.
historical_context: The poem first appeared in the Reflector, the quarterly Hunt edited for his brother John in 1810-11, and was expanded into a separate edition in 1814 as Hunt moved from journalism into open literary controversy. Its satiric guest-list engaged the quarrels over contemporary taste that would soon harden into Blackwood's and Quarterly attacks on Hunt and his circle, and Byron himself noted the poem in conversation.
literary_significance: The Feast of the Poets is a central document of Regency literary sociology and of the mock-heroic satire's survival into the Romantic period; its catalogue of presences and omissions shaped later nineteenth-century judgments about the literary field, and its blend of courtesy and critical edge typifies Hunt's contribution to Romantic periodical culture.
attribution_notes: Published by 'The Editor of the Examiner'; authorship by James Henry Leigh Hunt is established and undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published within The Reflector (1811); issued in expanded form as a separate work, The Feast of the Poets, with Notes, and Other Pieces in Verse, by the Editor of the Examiner, London, James Cawthorn, 1814, in octavo.
